specStatements.text: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. The temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
Changing the temperature of a gas, held at constant volume, changes the pressure exerted by the gas.
• explain how the motion of the molecules in a gas is related to both its temperature and its pressure
• explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.
A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. The pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface).
Students should be able to use the particle model to explain how increasing the volume in which a gas is contained, at constant temperature, can lead to a decrease in pressure.
For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature:
volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3

Students should be able to calculate the change in the pressure of a gas or the volume of a gas (a fixed mass held at constant temperature) when either the pressure or volume is increased or decreased.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas.
Students should be able to explain how, in a given situation eg a bicycle pump, doing work on an enclosed gas leads to an increase in the temperature of the gas.

scopeNotes.statement: • explain qualitatively the relation between the temperature of a gas and its pressure at constant volume.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for a qualitative explanation only, so this content states the direction of the change and its molecular cause — higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force, so the pressure rises, and the reverse on cooling. No proportionality between pressure and temperature is stated or implied, no pressure–temperature calculations are set, and the kelvin scale and absolute zero are not introduced here. The only calculations in this section are those the specification does require, using pressure × volume = constant at constant temperature.

concepts.definition: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with one another or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. A higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster on average. It is an average across the whole gas: at any instant some molecules are moving much faster than others.

Gas molecules collide with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall, and the pressure is the total force these collisions exert on each unit area of wall. Anything that makes the collisions more frequent, or makes each collision exert a greater force, increases the pressure.

concepts.term: Temperature and pressure at constant volume
concepts.definition: Changing the temperature of a gas, held at constant volume, changes the pressure exerted by the gas. Raising the temperature raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move faster: they strike the walls more often each second and each strike exerts a greater force, so the pressure rises. Cooling the gas does the reverse and the pressure falls.

The gas is sealed in a container whose size cannot change, such as a rigid metal can or a sealed glass flask. The gas cannot expand or contract, so any change in the pressure must come from a change in the motion of the molecules.

The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or to any surface placed in the gas. Individual molecules arrive at the surface from all directions, but the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out, leaving a combined force perpendicular to the surface.

concepts.term: Compression and expansion of a gas
concepts.definition: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Increasing the pressure acting on a gas squashes it into a smaller volume; reducing the pressure allows it to expand into a larger volume.

If the volume in which a fixed mass of gas is contained is increased while the temperature stays constant, the same number of molecules is spread through a larger space. The molecules travel further between hits on the walls, so each area of wall is struck less often each second and the pressure decreases. The molecules do not change speed, because the temperature has not changed.

concepts.term: Fixed mass held at a constant temperature
concepts.definition: The conditions under which pressure × volume = constant applies. The gas must be sealed so that no molecules enter or leave it (a fixed mass), and its temperature must not change during the compression or expansion. If either condition is broken, the product of pressure and volume is no longer constant.

For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature: pressure × volume = constant [p V = constant], where pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, is in metres cubed, m^3. Multiplying the pressure by the volume gives the same value before and after the change.
The unit of pressure. In p V = constant the pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa. A pressure in any other unit must be converted to pascals before the equation is used.

The unit of volume. In p V = constant the volume, V, is in metres cubed, m^3. A volume measured in cm^3 must be converted first, because 1 m^3 = 1 000 000 cm^3, so a volume in cm^3 is divided by 1 000 000 to give m^3.

concepts.term: Calculating a change in pressure or volume
concepts.definition: For a fixed mass of gas held at constant temperature the product p × V has the same value before and after a change. So multiply the starting pressure by the starting volume to find that constant, then divide it by the new volume to find the new pressure, or by the new pressure to find the new volume. Squeezing the gas into a smaller volume must give a larger pressure, and letting it expand must give a smaller one — a useful check on the answer.

Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves the object it acts on, energy is transferred, and that transfer is the work done. Work is a transfer of energy, not a store of energy that something holds.

Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas. The energy reaches the gas because a force pushes it and moves it, not because the gas has been heated by something hotter.

The energy stored inside the gas by its molecules — the total kinetic and potential energy of all of them. Increasing the internal energy of a gas by doing work on it raises the average kinetic energy of its molecules, and since temperature is related to that average kinetic energy, the temperature of the gas can rise.

concepts.term: Doing work on the gas in a bicycle pump
concepts.definition: When the piston of a bicycle pump is pushed in, the piston exerts a force on the enclosed gas and moves it, so work is done on the gas. Energy is transferred to the gas, its internal energy increases, the average kinetic energy of its molecules increases and the temperature of the gas rises — which is why the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm after several strokes.

misconceptions.question: A sealed rigid can of gas is warmed. Why does the pressure inside it rise?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they strike the walls more often and each strike exerts a greater force.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules themselves swell up when the gas is heated, and the bigger molecules press harder on the walls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet thermal expansion of solids and liquids first and carry 'heating makes things bigger' down to the particle scale. Diagrams that draw hot gas particles as larger circles reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: Heating changes how fast the molecules move, not how big they are. The size of a molecule does not change with temperature. It is the greater average kinetic energy — faster molecules, more frequent and harder collisions — that raises the pressure.

misconceptions.question: What is the temperature of a gas related to?
misconceptions.correct: The average kinetic energy of the molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature tells you the total kinetic energy of all the molecules added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Total' and 'average' both sound like ways of describing the whole gas, and students know that a bigger, hotter object stores more energy, so they fuse the two ideas.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: the temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. A large tank and a small flask of gas at the same temperature have the same average molecular kinetic energy, but the tank holds far more molecules and so far more energy in total.

misconceptions.question: Do all the molecules in a gas at one temperature move at the same speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. They move at a wide range of speeds; the temperature is related to the average kinetic energy.
misconceptions.misconception: At a given temperature every molecule in the gas is moving at the same speed, just in different directions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook animations often show identical particles moving at identical speeds, and 'random' is read as meaning random direction only.
misconceptions.correction: The motion is random in both direction and speed. Collisions constantly speed some molecules up and slow others down, so at any instant there is a spread of speeds. That is exactly why the specification speaks of the average kinetic energy.

misconceptions.question: In which direction does gas pressure produce a net force on a surface?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is in whatever direction the molecules happen to be travelling, so it acts at an angle along the wall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture one molecule striking the wall at a slant and generalise from that single impact instead of adding up the effect of enormous numbers of impacts from all directions.
misconceptions.correction: Molecules do arrive from every direction, but the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out. The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface).

misconceptions.question: Why does a gas exert a force on the lid of a sealed container above it?
misconceptions.correct: Because molecules in random motion collide with the lid, and those collisions produce a net force at right angles to it.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas pressure acts downwards, because gravity pulls the gas down onto whatever is beneath it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'pressure' is met first with solids resting on surfaces and with the weight of liquid columns, where the force really is the weight acting downwards.
misconceptions.correction: Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, which happen on every wall — top, bottom and sides. The net force on each surface is at right angles to that surface, so on a lid above the gas the force pushes upwards.

misconceptions.question: A gas expands into a larger volume at constant temperature. What happens to the speed of its molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing — the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy and the average speed are unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: When the gas is given more room the molecules slow down, and when it is squashed they speed up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly link crowding to more collisions, then wrongly assume the collisions themselves must be gentler or fiercer, because that is the only cause of a pressure change they can picture.
misconceptions.correction: At constant temperature the average kinetic energy is fixed, so the molecules keep the same average speed. What changes is how far they travel between hits on the walls, and therefore how often each area of wall is struck. Frequency of collisions, not their violence, explains the pressure change.

misconceptions.question: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has its volume halved. What happens to the pressure?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because pressure × volume must stay constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure and volume go together, so halving the volume halves the pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every relationship met before this one is direct proportion, so students expect 'one goes down, the other goes down' and read 'constant' as meaning the two quantities stay in step.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states pressure × volume = constant. Their product is fixed, so when one is halved the other must double. Check every answer against common sense: squashing a gas into a smaller space always raises its pressure.

misconceptions.question: Which units must be used in p V = constant?
misconceptions.correct: Pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not matter which volume unit you use, as long as you use the same one on both sides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In a two-state calculation the units often do cancel, so students who have only ever seen p1V1 = p2V2 conclude that units never matter and stop converting at all.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives the units: pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3. Quote the volume in m^3 as the specification requires, converting from cm^3 by dividing by 1 000 000.

misconceptions.question: Can the pressure of a gas change while its temperature stays the same?
misconceptions.correct: Yes — changing the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature changes its pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure can only change if the temperature changes, so if the question says the temperature is constant the pressure must be constant too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The temperature–pressure link at constant volume is usually taught first and taught hard, so 'temperature causes pressure' becomes the only mechanism students have.
misconceptions.correction: There are two separate situations in this section. At constant volume, changing the temperature changes the pressure. At constant temperature, changing the volume changes the pressure, and pressure × volume = constant lets you calculate the new value.

misconceptions.question: Why does the barrel of a bicycle pump get warm in use?
misconceptions.correct: Work is done on the enclosed gas, increasing its internal energy and its temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: It only gets warm because the piston rubs against the inside of the barrel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Friction is the standard explanation for anything that warms up when it is moved, and there really is some friction in a pump, so the answer feels safe.
misconceptions.correction: Friction plays a small part, but the effect the specification asks about is the work done on the gas itself. The force on the piston moves the gas, transferring energy to it, so its internal energy and temperature rise — the gas becomes hot even in a well-oiled pump.

misconceptions.question: What is work?
misconceptions.correct: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
misconceptions.misconception: Work and heating are just two words for the same thing — energy going into something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both do raise the internal energy of a gas, and both are described loosely as 'giving it energy', so students see no reason to keep the two apart.
misconceptions.correction: They are different transfers. Heating transfers energy because of a temperature difference; work transfers energy because a force moves something. A pump warms the gas by doing work on it, with no hotter object involved anywhere.

misconceptions.question: A gas is squashed quickly in a sealed container with no energy transferred by heating. Can its temperature rise?
misconceptions.correct: Yes — work is done on the gas, its internal energy increases and its temperature can increase.
misconceptions.misconception: The temperature cannot rise unless something hot is put in contact with the gas, because no heat has been added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature change is introduced through heating and cooling, so heating becomes the only route students accept to a hotter substance.
misconceptions.correction: Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas. Work is a second route by which energy reaches the gas, and it needs no hotter object at all.

misconceptions.question: A gas at constant volume is heated. How do its collisions with the walls change?
misconceptions.correct: The molecules hit the walls both more often each second and with a greater force.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecules hit the walls harder, but the number of hits each second stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that faster molecules hit harder and stop there, because the container is the same size so they cannot see why the number of hits would change.
misconceptions.correction: Faster molecules cross the container in less time, so they return to the walls more often as well as hitting harder. Both effects raise the pressure, and a full explanation names both.

misconceptions.question: Which collisions produce the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
misconceptions.correct: Collisions between the molecules and the walls of the container.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas pressure is caused by the molecules bumping into each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particle diagrams draw molecule-on-molecule collisions prominently, and 'pressure' in everyday speech sounds like crowding and jostling.
misconceptions.correction: Molecules do collide with one another, but pressure on a surface is the force from collisions with that surface. Explanations of a pressure change must talk about how often, and how hard, molecules hit the wall.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is the pressure p measured in p V = constant?
misconceptions.correct: In pascals, Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is a push, so it is measured in newtons like any other force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is taught as force spread over area and is described in class as a push, so the force unit sticks to it.
misconceptions.correction: Force is measured in newtons; pressure is force per unit area and is measured in pascals. The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa.

misconceptions.question: How many cm^3 are there in 1 m^3?
misconceptions.misconception: There are 1000 cm^3 in 1 m^3, just as there are 1000 mm in 1 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply a familiar length conversion to a volume without noticing that the factor between the units has to be cubed.
misconceptions.correction: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m^3 = 100 x 100 x 100 = 1 000 000 cm^3. To convert a volume from cm^3 into the m^3 the specification requires, divide by 1 000 000.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the internal energy of a gas when work is done on it?
misconceptions.correct: The internal energy of the gas increases, and this can cause its temperature to increase.
misconceptions.misconception: Internal energy is just another name for temperature, so saying both increase is saying the same thing twice.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two always seem to move together in classroom examples, and a thermometer is the only instrument students ever see pointed at the gas.
misconceptions.correction: They are different quantities. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules; temperature is related to their average kinetic energy. Doing work raises the internal energy, and that is what can raise the temperature.

misconceptions.question: A sealed rigid can of gas is warmed. What happens to the gas?
misconceptions.correct: Its volume cannot change, so its pressure rises instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating a gas always makes it expand, even when it is sealed inside a rigid can.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'heating makes gases expand' is met with balloons and syringes, where the container really can change size, and is then applied to every container.
misconceptions.correction: A gas expands on heating only if its container allows it. Held at constant volume, the gas cannot expand, so the faster molecules simply strike the walls more often and harder — and it is the pressure that rises.

misconceptions.question: What does 'constant' mean in pressure × volume = constant?
misconceptions.correct: The product of pressure and volume has the same value before and after the change.
misconceptions.misconception: It means pressure and volume add up to the same total, so if one falls by 5 the other rises by 5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Stays the same' is read as applying to a total, and adding is the operation students reach for first when two quantities have to balance.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is pressure × volume = constant. It is the product, not the sum, that is fixed, so the two quantities change by the same factor rather than by the same amount.

misconceptions.question: Is work something a gas contains?
misconceptions.correct: No. Work is the transfer of energy by a force; what a gas contains is internal energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Work is a type of energy stored inside an object, so a compressed gas holds a lot of work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is measured in joules like every energy store, so students file it alongside the stores rather than alongside the transfers.
misconceptions.correction: Work is a transfer, in the same family as heating, not a store. A compressed gas holds internal energy; work is how energy was transferred to it.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy that warms the gas in a bicycle pump come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the person pushing the piston, who does work on the enclosed gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Heat flows into the pump from the tyre, or from the warm hands gripping it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a hotter object as the source, because heating is the transfer they know best, and both the tyre and the hands are available candidates.
misconceptions.correction: The pump becomes warmer than both the tyre and the hands, so energy cannot be flowing in from them. The force on the piston moves the gas and does work on it, raising its internal energy and its temperature.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes the molecules of a gas and what the temperature of the gas tells you?

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to their average kinetic energy.
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: the molecules are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

options.text: They all travel at one fixed speed, and the temperature is related to that single shared speed.
options.rationale: Animations show identical particles moving identically, so students read 'random' as random direction only and expect one speed for all.

options.text: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to the total kinetic energy of the gas.
options.rationale: The first half is right, which makes it tempting; students who know a bigger hot object stores more energy substitute 'total' for 'average'.

options.text: They move along fixed paths, and the temperature is related to how far apart the molecules are.
options.rationale: Picks up the idea that hot gases are more spread out and treats spacing, rather than molecular motion, as what temperature measures.

mcqs.stem: A sealed metal can holds a gas. The can is rigid, so the volume of the gas cannot change. The can is warmed gently. Why does the pressure of the gas rise?

options.text: The molecules themselves swell as they warm, so they press more tightly on the walls.
options.rationale: Thermal expansion of solids is carried down to the particle scale, so students imagine the molecules growing rather than speeding up.

options.text: The molecules gain kinetic energy, so they strike the walls harder and more often each second.
options.rationale: Raising the temperature raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules; faster molecules collide with the walls both more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure rises.

options.text: The molecules strike the walls harder, but the number of strikes each second is unchanged.
options.rationale: A half-right answer: students see that faster molecules hit harder but assume a fixed-size container fixes the number of hits.

options.text: Warming makes the gas expand inside the can, and the expanding gas pushes on the walls.
options.rationale: 'Heating makes a gas expand' is applied even though the question states the volume cannot change.

mcqs.stem: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the wall of its container?

options.text: The weight of the gas pressing down on the wall, because gravity pulls the gas downwards.
options.rationale: Pressure is first met with solids and liquid columns, where the force really is a weight acting downwards.

options.text: The molecules repelling one another, pushing the outer ones firmly against the wall.
options.rationale: Locates the cause in molecule-to-molecule interaction rather than in collisions with the wall itself.

options.text: Molecules colliding with the wall, each collision exerting a small force on the wall.
options.rationale: Gas pressure is the combined effect of enormous numbers of molecular collisions with the wall, each exerting a small force over the area of the wall.

options.text: Molecules sliding along the wall, dragging on it in their own direction of travel.
options.rationale: Students who picture one molecule arriving at a slant expect a force along the wall rather than at right angles to it.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume is constant. Its temperature is lowered. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?

options.text: It stays the same, because the volume of the container has not been changed.
options.rationale: Students who tie pressure only to volume see no reason for it to change when the container is unchanged.

options.text: It falls, because the cooled molecules shrink and so press less on the walls.
options.rationale: The mirror image of 'heating swells the molecules'; the direction of the change is right, so it looks convincing.

options.text: It falls, because the molecules hit the walls with less force but just as often.
options.rationale: Half of the explanation is correct, and the predicted direction is correct, which makes this the strongest wrong answer.

options.text: It falls, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and with less force.
options.rationale: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules move more slowly: they reach the walls less frequently and each collision exerts a smaller force, so the pressure falls.

mcqs.stem: A flat plate is held inside a container of gas. In which direction does the gas pressure produce a net force on the plate?

options.text: A net force at right angles to the surface.
options.rationale: The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface); the sideways parts of the impacts cancel.

options.text: A net force straight downwards on the surface.
options.rationale: Gravity is assumed to set the direction, as it does for the pressure under a liquid or a solid block.

options.text: A net force slanted along the surface it strikes.
options.rationale: Follows from picturing a single molecule arriving at an angle instead of averaging over countless impacts.

options.text: A net force spread evenly in every direction at once.
options.rationale: Confuses the true statement that gas pressure acts on all surfaces with the direction of the force on one particular surface.

mcqs.stem: A sealed syringe contains a fixed mass of gas. The plunger is pulled out very slowly, so the temperature of the gas stays constant. Using the particle model, why does the pressure of the gas decrease?

options.text: The molecules slow down when given more room, so each strike on the wall is weaker.
options.rationale: Students assume a pressure change must mean a change in molecular speed, forgetting that constant temperature fixes the average kinetic energy.

options.text: The molecules spread through a bigger volume, so fewer hit each area of wall per second.
options.rationale: The same molecules, at the same average speed, travel further between collisions with the walls, so each area of wall is struck less often each second and the pressure falls.

options.text: The molecules are further apart, so they collide with one another far less often.
options.rationale: True as a statement about the gas, but it explains molecule-to-molecule collisions, not the collisions with the wall that produce the pressure.

options.text: The gas becomes thinner, so there is now less gas available to push on the walls.
options.rationale: Treats 'thinner' as meaning some gas has gone, although the syringe is sealed and the mass of gas is fixed.

mcqs.stem: Under which conditions does pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?

options.text: For any gas whose temperature is changing but whose mass is fixed.
options.rationale: Remembers the 'fixed mass' condition but not the constant temperature, and assumes a temperature change is what drives the pressure change.

options.text: For a fixed mass of gas held in a container of constant volume.
options.rationale: Imports the constant-volume condition from the temperature–pressure work in 4.3.3.1; at constant volume there is no volume change to calculate.

options.text: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature.
options.rationale: These are exactly the conditions the specification states before giving pressure × volume = constant.

options.text: For any gas in which the pressure and the volume increase together.
options.rationale: Direct-proportion thinking: students expect the two quantities to rise and fall in step.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas is held at a constant temperature. For this gas, p V = 24 (with p in Pa and V in m^3). Which pair of readings is possible for this gas?

options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'constant' as a fixed total: 20 + 4 = 24.
Both values scaled up together, as direct-proportion thinking expects; the product is 96, not 24.

options.text: p = 3 Pa, V = 2 m^3
options.rationale: Both values scaled down together; the product is 6, so the pair does not satisfy the equation.

options.text: p = 6 Pa, V = 4 m^3
options.rationale: 6 × 4 = 24, so this pair gives the required constant value of pressure × volume.

mcqs.stem: Which units must be used for pressure and volume in the equation p V = constant?

options.text: pressure in pascals, volume in metres cubed
options.rationale: The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.

options.text: pressure in newtons, volume in metres cubed
options.rationale: Pressure is described in class as a push, so the unit of force is attached to it.

options.text: pressure in pascals, volume in centimetres cubed
options.rationale: cm^3 is the volume unit used in most practical work, and students assume any consistent unit will do.

options.text: pressure in newtons, volume in centimetres cubed
options.rationale: Combines both errors, and is chosen by students working from laboratory habits rather than from the specified units.

mcqs.stem: A sealed container holds a gas in a volume of 5000 cm^3. What is this volume in the unit required by the equation p V = constant?

options.rationale: Divides by 1000, applying the millimetre-to-metre length factor to a volume.
The unit is simply relabelled, by students who believe the volume unit does not matter.
Divides by 10 000, a common slip when the conversion factor is half-remembered as 'ten thousand'.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.020 m^3 at a pressure of 150 000 Pa. It is compressed to a volume of 0.005 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?

options.rationale: The value of the constant, 150 000 × 0.020 = 3000, quoted as though it were the answer instead of being divided by the new volume.
The pressure is divided by four rather than multiplied by four, because pressure is assumed to fall as volume falls.
pV = 150 000 × 0.020 = 3000. The new pressure is 3000 ÷ 0.005 = 600 000 Pa — four times larger, as the volume is four times smaller.
Chosen by students who believe the pressure cannot change while the temperature is constant.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.60 m^3 at a pressure of 200 000 Pa. The pressure is reduced to 50 000 Pa. What is the new volume of the gas?

options.rationale: The volume is divided by four along with the pressure, as direct proportion would require.
The pressure ratio 200 000 ÷ 50 000 is quoted on its own, without multiplying by the starting volume.
Chosen by students who think nothing can change while the temperature is held constant.
pV = 200 000 × 0.60 = 120 000. The new volume is 120 000 ÷ 50 000 = 2.4 m^3 — four times larger, as the pressure is four times smaller.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what is meant by work?

options.text: Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition exactly: work is the transfer of energy by a force.

options.text: Work is the transfer of energy by heating.
options.rationale: Both transfers raise the internal energy of a gas, so students treat them as interchangeable.

options.text: Work is the energy stored inside a squashed gas.
options.rationale: Work is measured in joules, so it gets filed with the energy stores rather than with the transfers.

options.text: Work is the force needed to move an object.
options.rationale: Confuses work with the force itself; a force can act without any energy being transferred.

mcqs.stem: A gas is squashed quickly inside a sealed, well-insulated container, so no energy is transferred to it by heating. What happens to the gas?

options.text: Nothing changes its energy, because no energy is transferred by heating.
options.rationale: Heating is treated as the only way energy can reach a gas, so insulation is read as ruling out any change.

options.text: Work is done on it, so its internal energy rises and it can get hotter.
options.rationale: Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas — no heating is needed.

options.text: Its temperature rises, but the internal energy of the gas stays the same.
options.rationale: Written by students who treat temperature and internal energy as unrelated quantities that need not change together.

options.text: Its internal energy falls, because energy is used up squashing the gas.
options.rationale: 'Used up' language: the energy transferred by the force is thought to be spent rather than transferred to the gas.

mcqs.stem: After a tyre has been inflated, the barrel of the bicycle pump is noticeably warm — warmer than the tyre and warmer than the hands holding it. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Friction between the piston and barrel is the only cause of the warming.
options.rationale: Friction is the standard explanation for anything that warms up when moved, and a pump does have some friction.

options.text: Heat flows into the pump from the tyre and from the hands holding it.
options.rationale: Students look for a hotter object as the source, although the stem states the pump is the hottest of the three.

options.text: The piston does work on the gas, raising its internal energy and temperature.
options.rationale: The force on the piston moves the enclosed gas, so work is done on it. Its internal energy increases, the average kinetic energy of its molecules increases and its temperature rises.

options.text: The gas temperature rises although its internal energy does not change.
options.rationale: Separates temperature from internal energy, which students often treat as unconnected quantities.
